title: Barth's simple summary
hook: Karl Barth, asked to sum up his vast theology, is remembered for naming a children's song, Jesus loves me

segments.voice: Yesterday, George MacDonald: God's love as a thread too fine to see, and a fire that won't give up. Your line was love will not let go. Who did you show you haven't given up on? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

Karl Barth wrote theology by the shelf. His great work, the Church Dogmatics, fills thick volume after thick volume, and he never finished it. The story goes that on a lecture visit, a student asked him whether he could sum up his whole life's work in a single sentence. And Barth, the story says, answered with a song from childhood: "Jesus loves me! this I know, for the Bible tells me so." The story is told in more than one version, and people still argue about exactly where and when he said it. But it stuck, maybe because of the surprise in it. Today, Barth's simple summary.

It sounds like a dodge. It isn't. Barth's theology turns on one conviction: we don't climb up to God; God comes down to us. Everything starts with God speaking, God acting, God loving first, in Jesus Christ. That's why he argued so hard with theologians who began from human experience, Schleiermacher among them, whom this path met last week. Now look at the song word by word. Jesus: the center is a person, not an idea. Loves: the first thing God says to us is yes. Me: a person, not humanity in general. This I know, for the Bible tells me so: the knowing isn't something worked out alone; it was told, handed over, given. The first letter of John puts it the same way round: "We love him, because he first loved us." And, shorter still: "God is love." Barth's critics found him hard going, and sometimes too sure of himself. His admirers say the thick volumes are, in a way, one long commentary on that children's line. Christians read him both ways. Either way, the scene stays. A man who could talk for volumes, asked for the heart of it all, reached for words a child could sing.
screen: `GOD COMES DOWN FIRST` · `JESUS. LOVES. ME.` · `HE FIRST LOVED US` · `THE HEART, IN A CHILD'S SONG`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing it, or say it. Settle, and breathe. If you know the old children's song, sing the first line quietly, as slowly as you like: Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so. If singing feels strange, say it, or just hear it in your head. If you're here to learn rather than to pray, notice what each word claims, one at a time, without needing to agree. Let every word land before the next one comes. Then rest in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
Barth's simple summary. Karl Barth, the story says, summed up his vast theology with a children's song: Jesus loves me, this I know.
Your line: Jesus loves me. Today, when something feels complicated, try saying its heart in one sentence a child could understand. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: "Jesus Loves Me" is sung in Sunday schools and children's services across different churches, and some adults sing or say it as a short prayer of trust.
